questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct pronoun to fill the blank: Neither Ravi nor his brothers have submitted __________ assignments.
questions.explanation: 'Their' is correct because when 'neither...nor' connects a singular and a plural subject, the pronoun agrees with the nearer subject ('brothers' — plural), taking 'their'. 'His' is wrong because it agrees only with 'Ravi' (singular) and ignores the closer plural subject. 'Its' is wrong because it is used for non-living things, not people. 'Our' is wrong because it indicates first-person plural, but neither subject includes the speaker.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the correct sentence using the present perfect tense:
options: She has completed her homework already.
She is completing her homework already.
She will complete her homework already.
questions.correctAnswer: She has completed her homework already.
questions.explanation: 'She has completed' is present perfect (has/have + past participle), used with 'already' to indicate an action completed before now. 'She completed' is wrong — that is simple past tense, not present perfect. 'She is completing' is wrong — that is present continuous tense. 'She will complete' is wrong — that is simple future tense.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about pronouns:

(i) A reflexive pronoun refers back to the subject of the sentence.
(ii) 'Who' is used as a subject pronoun and 'whom' as an object pronoun.
(iii) 'It' can be used as a dummy subject in sentences about weather.
(iv) Possessive pronouns always need an apostrophe.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — reflexive pronouns (myself, himself, themselves) refer back to the subject (e.g., 'He hurt himself'). (ii) is correct — 'who' is subjective case and 'whom' is objective case (e.g., 'Who called?' vs 'Whom did you call?'). (iii) is correct — 'It' serves as a dummy/expletive subject in weather sentences ('It is raining'). (iv) is wrong — possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs) NEVER take an apostrophe; it is possessive ADJECTIVES and nouns that may use apostrophes.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: By the time we reached the station, the train __________.
questions.explanation: 'Had left' (past perfect) is correct because it describes an action completed before another past action ('reached'). The past perfect shows the earlier of two past events. 'Has left' is wrong — present perfect cannot be used when both actions are in the past. 'Left' is wrong — simple past would mean both actions happened simultaneously. 'Was leaving' is wrong — past continuous implies the train was in the process of leaving when they arrived, not already gone.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): 'Themselves' is a reflexive pronoun.
Reason (R): Reflexive pronouns end in '-self' (singular) or '-selves' (plural) and refer back to the subject.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — 'themselves' is indeed a reflexive pronoun (plural third person). Reason (R) is also correct — reflexive pronouns are formed by adding '-self' (singular: myself, yourself, himself) or '-selves' (plural: ourselves, yourselves, themselves) and they refer back to the subject. (R) explains (A) because 'themselves' ends in '-selves' and refers back to a plural subject, perfectly fitting the definition. Option 2 is wrong because (R) is the grammatical rule that proves (A). Option 3 is wrong because (R) is correct. Option 4 is wrong because (A) is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following pronouns with their types:

Column I:
(a) who
(b) myself
(c) this
(d) everyone

Column II:
(i) Demonstrative pronoun
(ii) Reflexive pronoun
(iii) Relative pronoun
(iv) Indefinite pronoun

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: (a) 'who' is a relative pronoun — it introduces a relative clause modifying a noun — matches (iii). (b) 'myself' is a reflexive pronoun — it refers back to the first-person subject — matches (ii). (c) 'this' is a demonstrative pronoun — it points to a specific thing — matches (i). (d) 'everyone' is an indefinite pronoun — it refers to people in general without specifying — matches (iv). Option 2 swaps 'who' and 'myself'. Option 3 swaps 'this' and 'everyone'. Option 4 swaps 'myself' and 'everyone'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the correct sentence in the simple future tense:
questions.explanation: 'They will arrive' uses 'will + base verb', which is the simple future tense structure. 'They are arriving' is wrong — that is present continuous used for planned future events, not simple future. 'They arrived' is wrong — that is simple past tense and contradicts 'tomorrow'. 'They have arrived' is wrong — that is present perfect and contradicts the future time marker 'tomorrow'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences uses a pronoun INCORRECTLY?

(i) Him and I went to the market.
(ii) The teacher asked her to sit down.
(iii) She gave the book to myself.
(iv) Each of the boys has done his work.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) is incorrect — 'Him' is an object pronoun used as a subject; correct form is 'He and I went to the market'. (iii) is incorrect — 'myself' is a reflexive pronoun and cannot replace 'me' after a preposition when the subject is different ('She gave the book to me' is correct). (ii) is correct — 'her' is properly used as an object pronoun after the verb 'asked'. (iv) is correct — 'each' is singular, so 'his' (singular possessive) correctly agrees with it.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct tense form: She __________ in this school since 2018.
questions.explanation: 'Has been teaching' (present perfect continuous) is correct because the action started in the past (2018) and is still continuing in the present, indicated by 'since'. 'Is teaching' is wrong — present continuous doesn't convey duration from a past point. 'Taught' is wrong — simple past implies the action is finished, contradicting 'since 2018' (which implies ongoing). 'Teaches' is wrong — simple present states a habit or fact but doesn't connect to a specific starting point in the past.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about tenses:

(i) The past perfect tense is formed using 'had + past participle'.
(ii) The present continuous tense is formed using 'is/am/are + present participle (-ing)'.
(iii) The simple future tense always uses 'shall' with all subjects.
(iv) The present perfect tense uses 'has/have + past participle'.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — past perfect: had + V3 (e.g., 'had gone', 'had written'). (ii) is correct — present continuous: am/is/are + V-ing (e.g., 'is running', 'are playing'). (iv) is correct — present perfect: has/have + V3 (e.g., 'has eaten', 'have finished'). (iii) is wrong — 'shall' is traditionally used with 'I' and 'we', while 'will' is used with all other subjects (he, she, it, they, you); in modern usage, 'will' is used with all subjects.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the relative pronoun in the sentence: 'The student whose bag was stolen reported to the police.'
questions.explanation: 'Whose' is the relative pronoun — it introduces the relative clause 'whose bag was stolen' and shows possession while referring to 'the student'. 'The' is wrong — it is a definite article. 'Was' is wrong — it is an auxiliary verb in the passive construction. 'Reported' is wrong — it is the main verb of the principal clause.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the sentence 'It is raining heavily', 'it' does not refer to any specific noun.
Reason (R): 'It' is used as an impersonal or dummy subject in sentences describing weather, time, or distance.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — in 'It is raining', 'it' doesn't refer to any particular person or thing. Reason (R) is also correct — English uses 'it' as a dummy subject for weather (It is cold), time (It is 5 o'clock), and distance (It is 10 km). (R) explains (A) because the 'it' in the sentence is being used in this impersonal way. Option 2 is wrong because (R) gives the exact grammatical reason for (A). Option 3 is wrong because (R) is correct. Option 4 is wrong because (A) is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct option: The committee members could not agree among __________.
questions.explanation: 'Themselves' is correct because the subject 'committee members' (plural) is the same as the object — a reflexive pronoun is needed, and 'themselves' matches the plural subject. 'Them' is wrong — a non-reflexive object pronoun cannot be used when subject and object are the same entity. 'Itself' is wrong — it is singular and refers to non-living things or collectives treated as one unit. 'Oneself' is wrong — it is used with the indefinite pronoun 'one', not with a specific plural noun.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following sentences with the correct tense names:

Column I:
(a) She writes a letter every day.
(b) She was writing a letter when I called.
(c) She will have written the letter by tomorrow.
(d) She has been writing letters since morning.

Column II:
(i) Past continuous
(ii) Simple present
(iii) Present perfect continuous
(iv) Future perfect

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: (a) 'writes' — base verb with habitual 'every day' = Simple Present — matches (ii). (b) 'was writing...when I called' — action in progress interrupted by another past action = Past Continuous — matches (i). (c) 'will have written...by tomorrow' — action to be completed before a future deadline = Future Perfect — matches (iv). (d) 'has been writing...since morning' — action started in the past, still continuing = Present Perfect Continuous — matches (iii). Option 2 swaps (a) and (b). Option 3 swaps (c) and (d). Option 4 incorrectly assigns past continuous to (c).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the sentence with the correct use of the past continuous tense:
options: The children were playing in the park when it started raining.
The children played in the park when it started raining.
The children had played in the park when it started raining.
The children have been playing in the park when it started raining.
questions.correctAnswer: The children were playing in the park when it started raining.
questions.explanation: 'Were playing' (past continuous) correctly describes an ongoing action interrupted by another past event ('started raining'). 'Played' (simple past) is wrong — it implies a completed action, not one in progress when the rain began. 'Had played' (past perfect) is wrong — it implies they finished playing before the rain, not that they were in the middle of playing. 'Have been playing' (present perfect continuous) is wrong — it mixes present relevance with a past time reference ('started'), which is grammatically inconsistent.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the pronoun 'it':

(i) 'It' can refer to animals whose gender is unknown.
(ii) 'It' can refer to babies whose gender is not known.
(iii) 'It' is always used for non-living things only.
(iv) 'It' can be used as an anticipatory subject.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'it' is used for animals when gender is unspecified ('The cat licked its paw'). (ii) is correct — 'it' may be used for a baby when gender is unknown ('The baby is in its crib'). (iv) is correct — 'it' can serve as an anticipatory subject ('It is important to study well' — 'it' anticipates the real subject 'to study well'). (iii) is wrong — as shown in (i) and (ii), 'it' is NOT restricted to non-living things; it can refer to animals, babies, and serve grammatical functions.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct option: __________ of the two sisters is taller?
questions.explanation: 'Which' is correct because when choosing from a specific, limited group (two sisters), 'which' is used as an interrogative pronoun. 'Who' is wrong — 'who' asks about identity in general, not for selection from a defined group. 'Whom' is wrong — 'whom' is used as an object pronoun and the question needs a subject. 'What' is wrong — 'what' asks about things or concepts, not about persons in a comparison.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The present perfect tense cannot be used with definite past time expressions like 'yesterday' or 'last week'.
Reason (R): The present perfect tense connects a past action to the present moment, while definite past time markers anchor the action entirely in the past.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — we cannot say 'I have gone yesterday' (must use 'I went yesterday'). Reason (R) is also correct — the present perfect links past to present ('I have finished' = result relevant now), while 'yesterday' places everything in the closed past. (R) explains (A) because the conflict between present-relevance and definite-past markers is exactly why they cannot coexist. Option 2 is wrong because (R) provides the linguistic explanation. Option 3 is wrong because (R) is grammatically accurate. Option 4 is wrong because (A) is a standard English grammar rule.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the correct pronoun: Let you and __________ do this work together.
questions.explanation: 'Me' is correct because after 'let' the objective case is required (Let + object pronoun); 'Let you and me' is the standard construction. 'I' is wrong — 'I' is the subjective case and cannot follow 'let' (which takes objects). 'Myself' is wrong — reflexive pronouns should not be used as standalone objects after 'let' without a preceding subject 'I'. 'Mine' is wrong — 'mine' is a possessive pronoun and cannot function as an object of 'let'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences are in the future continuous tense?

(i) She will be waiting for you at the airport.
(ii) They will have completed the project by Friday.
(iii) I will be travelling to Delhi next week.
(iv) He will go to the office tomorrow.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) 'will be waiting' = will + be + V-ing = future continuous ✓. (iii) 'will be travelling' = will + be + V-ing = future continuous ✓. (ii) 'will have completed' = will + have + V3 = future PERFECT, not continuous. (iv) 'will go' = will + base verb = simple future, not continuous. Therefore only (i) and (iii) are future continuous.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: Each of the students must bring __________ own textbook to class.
questions.explanation: 'His or her' is correct because 'each' is a singular indefinite pronoun requiring a singular possessive pronoun in formal grammar. 'Their' is wrong in formal/traditional grammar — 'each' is singular and strictly requires a singular pronoun (though modern informal English accepts 'their'). 'Its' is wrong because it refers to non-living things, not students. 'Our' is wrong because it is first-person plural, while 'each' refers to third-person subjects.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following tense forms with their structures:

Column I:
(a) Present Perfect Continuous
(b) Past Perfect
(c) Future Perfect
(d) Past Continuous

Column II:
(i) had + past participle
(ii) was/were + V-ing
(iii) will have + past participle
(iv) has/have been + V-ing

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: (a) Present Perfect Continuous = has/have been + V-ing (e.g., 'has been running') — matches (iv). (b) Past Perfect = had + past participle (e.g., 'had gone') — matches (i). (c) Future Perfect = will have + past participle (e.g., 'will have finished') — matches (iii). (d) Past Continuous = was/were + V-ing (e.g., 'was sleeping') — matches (ii). Option 2 swaps (a) and (b). Option 3 swaps (c) and (d). Option 4 swaps (b) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct sentence:
options: He and I are going to the market.
Him and me are going to the market.
Me and him are going to the market.
Him and I are going to the market.
questions.correctAnswer: He and I are going to the market.
questions.explanation: 'He and I' is correct because both are subjects of the verb 'are going' and must be in the subjective case (He = subjective; I = subjective). 'Him and me' is wrong — both are objective case pronouns used incorrectly as subjects. 'Me and him' is wrong — same error plus incorrect etiquette (first person should come last). 'Him and I' is wrong — 'Him' is objective case and cannot be a subject.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the past perfect tense:

(i) It describes an action completed before another past action.
(ii) Its structure is: had + past participle.
(iii) It can be used with time expressions like 'before', 'after', 'by the time'.
(iv) It is used for habitual past actions.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — the past perfect shows the 'earlier past' relative to another past event. (ii) is correct — its formula is had + V3 (e.g., 'had eaten', 'had left'). (iii) is correct — time connectors like 'before', 'after', 'by the time', 'already' commonly signal past perfect usage. (iv) is wrong — habitual past actions are expressed by 'used to + verb' or 'would + verb', not by the past perfect.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the correct pronoun: The dog wagged __________ tail happily.
questions.explanation: 'Its' (possessive pronoun without apostrophe) is correct because it shows possession by the dog. 'It's' is wrong — 'it's' is a contraction of 'it is' or 'it has', not a possessive form. 'His' is wrong — 'his' refers to a male person; for animals whose gender is unspecified, 'its' is standard. 'Their' is wrong — 'their' is plural, but only one dog is mentioned.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): We say 'Whom did you meet?' and not 'Who did you meet?' in formal grammar.
Reason (R): 'Whom' is used when the pronoun functions as the object of a verb or preposition.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — in formal grammar, 'Whom did you meet?' is the prescribed form. Reason (R) is also correct — 'whom' is the objective case of 'who' and is used when the pronoun is the object of the verb ('meet') or a preposition. (R) explains (A) because in the sentence, the pronoun is the object of 'meet' (you met HIM, not HE), hence 'whom' is required. Option 2 is wrong because (R) directly explains (A). Option 3 is wrong because (R) is a valid grammar rule. Option 4 is wrong because (A) is correct in formal usage.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the tense of the underlined verb: 'The children have been playing since 3 o'clock.'
questions.explanation: 'Have been playing' = have/has + been + V-ing, which is the Present Perfect Continuous tense, used for actions that started in the past and are still continuing (indicated by 'since 3 o'clock'). Present Continuous is wrong — that would be 'are playing' (no 'have been'). Past Perfect Continuous is wrong — that would be 'had been playing'. Present Perfect is wrong — that would be 'have played' (without 'been' and '-ing').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following are demonstrative pronouns?

(i) this
(ii) those
(iii) who
(iv) that (when pointing to something)

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) 'this' — points to a nearby singular thing = demonstrative pronoun ✓. (ii) 'those' — points to distant plural things = demonstrative pronoun ✓. (iv) 'that' — when used to point to something specific = demonstrative pronoun ✓ (the four demonstratives are: this, that, these, those). (iii) 'who' is wrong — 'who' is an interrogative or relative pronoun, not a demonstrative pronoun.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct form: If I __________ you, I would not accept this offer.
questions.explanation: 'Were' is correct because this is a Type 2 conditional (present unreal/hypothetical). In formal English, 'were' (subjunctive) is used for all persons in unreal conditions ('If I were', 'If he were'). 'Was' is wrong — though colloquially used, formal grammar requires 'were' in the subjunctive after 'if' for hypothetical situations. 'Am' is wrong — present tense cannot be used in a hypothetical/unreal condition. 'Had been' is wrong — that would create a Type 3 conditional referring to an unreal past, not the present hypothetical.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about personal pronouns:

(i) 'I', 'we' are first-person pronouns.
(ii) 'You' is the only pronoun that is the same in both singular and plural.
(iii) 'They' is always used for plural subjects only.
(iv) 'He', 'she', 'it' are third-person singular pronouns.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'I' (singular) and 'we' (plural) are first-person pronouns referring to the speaker(s). (ii) is correct — 'you' serves as both singular and plural second-person pronoun with no change in form. (iv) is correct — 'he' (male), 'she' (female), 'it' (neuter) are all third-person singular pronouns. (iii) is wrong — in modern English, 'they' is also accepted as a singular pronoun for a person of unspecified gender ('Someone left their bag').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the correct option: When I entered the room, she __________ a novel.
questions.explanation: 'Was reading' (past continuous) correctly describes an action in progress at the time another past action occurred ('entered'). 'Read' (simple past) is wrong — it implies a completed action, not one in progress when interrupted. 'Has read' (present perfect) is wrong — it cannot be used with a past time reference ('when I entered'). 'Reads' (simple present) is wrong — the sentence describes past events.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following sentences with the type of pronoun used:

Column I:
(a) She hurt herself.
(b) This is my book.
(c) Someone is at the door.
(d) The man who came is my uncle.

Column II:
(i) Indefinite pronoun
(ii) Relative pronoun
(iii) Demonstrative pronoun
(iv) Reflexive pronoun

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: (a) 'herself' is a reflexive pronoun (reflects back to 'she') — matches (iv). (b) 'This' is a demonstrative pronoun (points to a specific book) — matches (iii). (c) 'Someone' is an indefinite pronoun (refers to an unspecified person) — matches (i). (d) 'who' is a relative pronoun (introduces the relative clause 'who came') — matches (ii). Option 2 swaps reflexive and demonstrative. Option 3 swaps indefinite and relative. Option 4 swaps demonstrative and indefinite.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct tense: By next March, she __________ her graduation.
questions.explanation: 'Will have completed' (future perfect) is correct because 'by next March' indicates an action that will be finished before a specified future point. 'Will complete' is wrong — simple future doesn't emphasize completion before a deadline. 'Has completed' is wrong — present perfect is for past-to-present connections, not future. 'Is completing' is wrong — present continuous doesn't express completion by a future date.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The pronoun must agree with its antecedent in number and gender.
Reason (R): A pronoun replaces a noun (its antecedent) and must match it to avoid ambiguity.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — pronouns must agree with antecedents in number (singular/plural) and gender (he/she/it). Reason (R) is also correct — pronouns replace nouns and must match them to maintain clarity. (R) explains (A): the need for agreement arises precisely because the pronoun represents the noun, and mismatching would create confusion about what is being referred to. Option 2 is wrong because (R) gives the logical reason for (A). Option 3 is wrong because (R) is correct. Option 4 is wrong because (A) is a standard grammar rule.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the error in the sentence: 'Everyone should bring their own lunch to the picnic.'
options: 'Everyone' is singular but 'their' is plural — correct form is 'his or her'
There is no error in the sentence
questions.correctAnswer: 'Everyone' is singular but 'their' is plural — correct form is 'his or her'
questions.explanation: In traditional formal grammar, 'everyone' is singular and requires the singular pronoun 'his or her' (not plural 'their'). The correct formal version is: 'Everyone should bring his or her own lunch.' 'No error' is wrong — while modern informal English accepts singular 'they', formal grammar rules (tested in competitive exams) flag this as a pronoun-antecedent disagreement. 'Should be must' is wrong — 'should' is grammatically correct here. 'Own is incorrectly placed' is wrong — 'own' correctly follows the possessive pronoun.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the future tense:

(i) 'Going to + verb' is used for planned future actions.
(ii) The present continuous can be used for fixed future arrangements.
(iii) 'Will' is always used for pre-planned actions.
(iv) The future continuous tense uses 'will be + V-ing'.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'going to' expresses intentions and planned actions ('I am going to study medicine'). (ii) is correct — present continuous can express fixed future arrangements ('We are meeting at 5 PM tomorrow'). (iv) is correct — future continuous = will + be + V-ing ('She will be sleeping at midnight'). (iii) is wrong — 'will' is actually used more for spontaneous decisions and predictions, NOT pre-planned actions; pre-planned actions use 'going to' or present continuous.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct pronoun: The manager himself __________ announced the decision.
questions.explanation: 'Has' is correct because the subject is 'the manager' (singular third person), which takes 'has'. 'Himself' is an emphatic/intensive pronoun that does not change the number of the subject. 'Have' is wrong — it is used with plural subjects or 'I/you'. 'Are' is wrong — the sentence requires an auxiliary verb for present perfect or a main verb, and 'are' doesn't fit. 'Were' is wrong — it is plural past tense and doesn't match the singular present context.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences correctly use the simple past tense?

(i) She went to the market yesterday.
(ii) He has eaten breakfast an hour ago.
(iii) They watched the movie last night.
(iv) We visited Srinagar last summer.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) 'went' + 'yesterday' = simple past ✓. (iii) 'watched' + 'last night' = simple past ✓. (iv) 'visited' + 'last summer' = simple past ✓. (ii) is wrong — 'has eaten' is present perfect, which cannot be used with a definite past time marker ('an hour ago'). The correct form would be 'He ate breakfast an hour ago'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the correct option: This is the woman __________ son won the scholarship.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' is correct because it shows possession — the son belongs to the woman. 'Whose' is the possessive form of the relative pronoun used for people. 'Who' is wrong — it is a subject pronoun and cannot show possession (we cannot say 'who son'). 'Whom' is wrong — it is an object pronoun and cannot show possession. 'Which' is wrong — it is used for things/animals, not for people.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following pronouns with their cases:

Column I:
(a) She
(b) Her (in 'I saw her')
(c) Hers
(d) Herself

Column II:
(i) Possessive case
(ii) Reflexive
(iii) Nominative (subjective) case
(iv) Objective (accusative) case

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: (a) 'She' is used as a subject = nominative case — matches (iii). (b) 'Her' (as object in 'I saw her') = objective/accusative case — matches (iv). (c) 'Hers' shows ownership without a following noun = possessive case — matches (i). (d) 'Herself' reflects back to the subject = reflexive — matches (ii). Option 2 swaps nominative and objective. Option 3 swaps possessive and reflexive. Option 4 swaps objective and possessive.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct tense: I __________ in this city for ten years now.
questions.explanation: 'Have been living' (present perfect continuous) is correct because the action started in the past ('ten years ago') and continues into the present (indicated by 'now'). 'Am living' is wrong — present continuous doesn't express duration from a specific past point. 'Lived' is wrong — simple past implies the action is finished, contradicting 'now'. 'Was living' is wrong — past continuous describes a past-only action, not one continuing to the present.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about relative pronouns:

(i) 'Who' is used for persons.
(ii) 'Which' is used for things and animals.
(iii) 'That' can be used for both persons and things.
(iv) 'Whom' is used as a subject in relative clauses.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'who' is the relative pronoun for persons ('The man who came...'). (ii) is correct — 'which' is used for things and animals ('The book which I read...'). (iii) is correct — 'that' can refer to both persons and things ('The student that topped...' / 'The car that I bought...'). (iv) is wrong — 'whom' is used as an OBJECT in relative clauses, not as a subject; 'who' is the subject form.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): We use the past continuous tense to describe two actions happening simultaneously in the past.
Reason (R): The past continuous tense (was/were + V-ing) describes an ongoing action at a particular time in the past.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — past continuous is used for simultaneous past actions ('While I was cooking, she was reading'). Reason (R) is also correct — past continuous describes actions in progress at a past time. (R) explains (A) because if the tense describes ongoing actions at a particular time, then two such ongoing actions at the same time would both use past continuous — confirming (A). Option 2 is wrong because (R) is the underlying rule that supports (A). Option 3 is wrong because (R) is grammatically correct. Option 4 is wrong because (A) is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the correct pronoun: It was __________ who broke the window.
questions.explanation: 'He' is correct because after the verb 'to be' (was), a subject complement takes the nominative/subjective case in formal grammar ('It was he' = 'He was it'). 'Him' is wrong — though commonly used in informal speech, formal grammar requires the subjective case after 'be' verbs. 'His' is wrong — it is possessive and doesn't fit the structure. 'Himself' is wrong — reflexive pronouns need a subject they refer back to, and 'it' (dummy subject) cannot serve as that antecedent here.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following are examples of interrogative pronouns?

(i) Who
(ii) Whom
(iii) Where
(iv) What

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) 'Who' is an interrogative pronoun — used to ask about people ('Who is there?'). (ii) 'Whom' is an interrogative pronoun — objective case of 'who' ('Whom did you call?'). (iv) 'What' is an interrogative pronoun — used to ask about things ('What is this?'). (iii) 'Where' is wrong — 'where' is an interrogative ADVERB (asks about place), not a pronoun. Interrogative pronouns replace nouns; adverbs modify verbs.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct option: The teacher asked who __________ the answer.
questions.explanation: 'Knew' (simple past) is correct because the reporting verb 'asked' is in the past tense, so the verb in the reported clause must also be in the past tense (sequence/backshift of tenses). 'Knows' is wrong — present tense breaks the sequence after a past-tense reporting verb. 'Know' is wrong — bare infinitive doesn't fit after 'who' in this indirect question structure. 'Is knowing' is wrong — 'know' is a stative verb that is not normally used in continuous tenses.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the sequence of tenses:

(i) If the main clause is in the past tense, the subordinate clause usually takes a past tense.
(ii) Universal truths remain in the present tense regardless of the main clause.
(iii) If the main clause is in the present tense, the subordinate clause can be in any tense.
(iv) Future tense in the subordinate clause is never changed.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — when the main verb is past, the subordinate verb typically shifts to past ('He said he was tired'). (ii) is correct — universal truths stay in present tense ('He said the Earth revolves around the Sun'). (iii) is correct — with a present/future main verb, the subordinate clause can take any tense logically needed. (iv) is wrong — future tense IS changed during backshift; 'will' becomes 'would' in reported speech ('He said he would come').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: Neither of the girls has brought __________ umbrella.
questions.explanation: 'Her' is correct because 'neither' is singular (meaning 'not one and not the other'), and since the antecedent is 'girls' (female), the singular feminine possessive 'her' is required. 'Their' is wrong — 'neither' takes a singular pronoun in formal grammar. 'Its' is wrong — it refers to non-living things or animals, not to girls. 'Our' is wrong — first-person plural has no connection to the third-person subject.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following tenses with their correct usage:

Column I:
(a) Simple Present
(b) Present Perfect
(c) Simple Past
(d) Past Perfect

Column II:
(i) An action completed before another past action
(ii) A habitual or regular action
(iii) A completed action with present relevance
(iv) A completed action at a definite past time

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: (a) Simple Present — used for habits, routines, general truths — matches (ii). (b) Present Perfect — past action whose result matters now — matches (iii). (c) Simple Past — a completed action at a specific past time (yesterday, last year) — matches (iv). (d) Past Perfect — the 'earlier past', completed before another past event — matches (i). Option 2 swaps (a) and (b). Option 3 swaps (c) and (d). Option 4 swaps (b) and (c).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the correct sentence:
options: She has been working here since five years.
She has been working here for five years.
She has been working here from five years.
She is working here since five years.
questions.correctAnswer: She has been working here for five years.
questions.explanation: 'For five years' is correct because 'for' is used with a duration of time (five years, two hours, three months). 'Since five years' is wrong — 'since' is used with a point in time (since 2019, since Monday), not a duration. 'From five years' is wrong — 'from' is not used with the perfect tense in this way. 'Is working...since' is wrong — present continuous cannot be used with 'since' to show duration; the present perfect continuous ('has been working') is required.
